"X's Y" / "the Y of X": attach the genitive prefix የ (ya-) to the owner, then name the thing owned. The owner always comes first.

examples.english: an Amharic book (a book of Amharic)

description: "the [noun] who/that [did something]": build a past-tense relative clause by adding የ (ya-) to the perfective (past) verb; the definite ending -ው (-w) links it to the noun that follows.
"the [noun] who/that [does something]": build a present/habitual relative clause with the prefix የሚ (yammi-) on the imperfect verb, placed before the noun it describes.

Make a PAST-tense (perfect) verb negative — 'I didn't ...'. Take the affirmative perfect verb and wrap it: add the prefix አል (al-) and the suffix ም (-m). Turns hedku 'I went' into alhedkum 'I didn't go'.

examples.english: I didn't go to the market

description: Make a PRESENT/FUTURE (imperfect) verb negative — 'I don't / won't ...'. Drop the affirmative ending (-alahu 'I', -al 'he'), then wrap the verb with negative a- fused to the person marker (I = አል al-, he = አይ ay-, she/you = አት at-) plus the suffix ም (-m). Turns ifaligalahu 'I want' into alfaligim 'I don't want'.

Say something is NOT so with the negative copula አይደለም (aydallam) — the opposite of ነው (naw, 'is'). It agrees with the subject: I am not = አይደለሁም, he/it is not = አይደለም, she is not = አይደለችም, they are not = አይደሉም.

Present habitual / future: the imperfect verb takes the '-allä' auxiliary (from 'to exist'). One form covers both 'I go' and 'I will go'. The ending agrees with the subject: -alahu (I), -alah (you m), -al (he), -alan (we), -alu (they).
'I have [done]' — present perfect. Built on the verb's gerund (converb) stem plus the '-allä' auxiliary. Result state of a completed action. Examples are all 1st-person singular ('I have ...').
'I was [doing]' / 'I used to [do]' — the simple (bare) imperfect verb followed by ነበር näbbär ('was'). Expresses an ongoing or repeated action in the past. Here näbbär stays invariant for all persons.

examples.english: I used to go / I was going
you used to go / you were going (m)
he used to go / he was going
we used to go / we were going

description: Present/habitual (imperfective) conjugation of common verbs: 'I ___' takes the እ- prefix with the -አለሁ ending; 'you (m.) ___' takes the ት- prefix with the -አለህ ending. Renders the ESSENTIAL VERBS conjugation table from the source (infinitives already ship as vocab; these conjugated forms do not).
Your (m.) / his / her + [noun]. Completes the possessive-pronoun set beyond the app's existing 'my' (የኔ) and 'your (formal)' (የርስዎ) patterns.
template: ya anta / ya issu / ya isswa + [noun]

Also / too. The suffix -ም (-m) attaches to a pronoun (or noun) to add the meaning 'also/too'. The rest of the sentence stays unchanged.

State the hour by placing the number before ሰዓት (saat, 'o'clock/hour'). Add ከሩብ for quarter past, ተኩል for half past, ከ + minutes for minutes past, or ለ … [minutes] ጉዳይ for minutes to the hour. Note that Ethiopian hours are counted from sunrise, so add ~6 hours to convert to Western clock time.
structure: [number] + ሰዓት (+ ከሩብ / ተኩል / ከ [minutes] / ለ … [minutes] ጉዳይ)
template: [number] + saat (+ karub / takul / ka [minutes] / la … [minutes] guday)

description: Form ordinal numbers ('first', 'second', 'third' …) by adding the suffix -ኛ (-nya) to the cardinal number.
Amharic forms the name of a language by adding the suffix -ኛ (-nya) to the name of the people or region who speak it.
Many physical feelings are expressed as a single verb with the person marked as an object suffix (-ኝ, '...me'), so 'I'm hungry' is literally 'it hungered me'. You only need one word.

Second-person present-tense verb questions change their ending by the gender of the person addressed: -alah (ኧህ) when speaking to a man, -alesh/-iyalesh (ኧሽ) when speaking to a woman. The verb stem and the object stay the same. This m/f contrast recurs throughout the chapter.
structure: [object] + ti[verb]alah? (to a man)  |  [object] + ti[verb](i)yalesh? (to a woman)

description: I don't eat [food] — for stating dietary restrictions when ordering
Please bring me [item] — polite request to a waiter (m/f addressee)

examples.english: Please bring the menu (to a woman)

description: X is more [adjective] than Y — place ከ (ka, 'from/than') between the two things being compared, then the adjective + ነው.

examples.english: Trousers are better than a dress

description: the -est / most [adjective] — use በጣም (batam, 'very') before the adjective and attach the definite article (-ው/-ዋ) to the adjective.
Mark a noun plural (only when the count isn't clear from context) by adding -ኦች (-och) after a consonant or -ዎች (-woch) after a vowel.
structure: [noun ending in consonant] + ኦች  /  [noun ending in vowel] + ዎች

description: Show possession by attaching a suffix directly to the noun (an alternative to the analytic የኔ/yane form): -ኤ my, -ህ your(m), -ሽ your(f), -ው his, -ዋ her, -ችን our.
I want to [do something] — use the infinitive (መ-/ማ- form) followed by እፈልጋለሁ. Contrast the app's noun pattern '[noun] + ifaligalahu' (I want [a thing]).
Join words or clauses: እና (ina) 'and', ወይም (waym) 'or', ግን (gin) 'but'. እና may attach as the suffix -ና after a word ending in a vowel.

examples.amharic: ጥሩ ነው ግን በጣም ውድ ነው
examples.transliteration: tiru naw gin batam wid naw

description: State that something is NOT the case with አይደለም (aydallam, 'it isn't'). Distinct from የለም (yallam, 'there isn't') already in the app.
Physical sensations are expressed as a verb acting on 'me' (object suffix -ኝ = me), not as 'to be' + adjective. So 'I'm hot' is literally 'it-heats-me'.
Amharic often builds the object into the verb with a suffix instead of a separate word: -ው/-ዋ 'it/him', -ኣት 'her/it'. 'I want' + it collapses into one word.

Form quick 'Who/What/Why … is it?' questions by placing the question word before ነው? (naw?). A raised tone marks the question — there's no word reordering as in English. (Adds the interrogative ማን 'who', which the app lacks.)
Prepositions attach to the front of the noun: በ (ba) 'in/by/with', ለ (la) 'for/to', ከ (ka) 'from', ወደ (wada) 'to(ward)'.
